column4: Within one ayah, the garden’s rivers of unspoiled water and other drinks are set against people made to drink boiling water; it condenses the section’s two-source polarity.
The criminals move between Hell and حَمِيمٍ ءَانٍ, the exact endpoint-hot counterpart to the source section’s flowing garden spring.
The two gardens contain two springs that flow, فِيهِمَا عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ; both noun and motion directly amplify the section’s renewing spring.
Silver ءَانِيَة vessels and أَكْوَاب cups are circulated together; this is the source section’s exact vessel homograph beside its exact cup noun.
Cups, ewers, and a cup from مَعِين join vessel to visible flowing source; later hot drinking in this surah supplies the opposing water.
The commanded question asks who could bring مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ if human water sank away, making the section’s ready flowing spring an explicitly divine provision.
God’s servants drink from a spring and make it gush wherever they wish, joining drinking, spring, motion, and water placed at the garden people’s disposal.
A cup from مَعِين is passed around the garden; this same surah later gives the people of Hell a mixture of boiling water.
Golden dishes and أَكْوَاب are passed around the garden inhabitants, staging the source section’s cups as already supplied and served.
Garden companions pass a cup among themselves with neither idle speech nor sin in it, linking the prepared cup to the larger surah 88 garden scene without futile speech.
The garden has a brimming cup; in the same surah, the people of Hell have no drink except boiling water and foul fluid.
The second pair of gardens also has two springs, now described as gushing; this preserves the paired-spring scene while varying the kind of motion.
They are given drink from a ginger-mixed cup, repeating the source section’s passive giving-to-drink while changing the source from torment to reward.
This ayah identifies the source of the preceding cup as a garden spring called Salsabil, completing the cup-to-spring relation.
The righteous are given sealed pure drink, repeating the source section’s passive drinking formula with a protected garden beverage rather than endpoint-hot water.
Tasnim is identified as a spring from which those brought near drink, completing the drink-and-source sequence begun at 83:25.
Two gardens belong to the one who fears standing before the Lord; this identifies the stance of those whose two flowing springs appear at 55:50, opposite the criminals at 55:44.
The river test uses يَطْعَمْهُ for tasting or drinking its water, directly witnessing the source section’s dictionary claim that the ط ع م field extends to water.
Abraham names the Lord as the one who feeds him and gives him drink, pairing the two acts that the section reads as one table and locating their source in God.
Twelve springs burst from the struck stone, every group knows its drinking place, and the people are told to eat and drink from God’s provision.
Twelve springs gush from the rock and each tribe knows its drinking place, coupling a moving source with apportioned, ready access to water.
God sends water down and conducts it through the earth as springs, a direct account of the hidden source and renewed movement behind visible flowing water.
Gardens of palms and grapes have springs made to gush within them, reproducing the garden-and-spring scene in the world as a sign.
Water descends in due measure, is lodged in the earth, and can be taken away; it states both the hidden storage and divine control presupposed by the ready spring.
God sends water from the sky, gives it to people to drink, and says they are not its keepers; the drink is ready, but its source is not theirs to command.
The hearers are made to look at the very water they drink, turning the garden cup’s contents into a question about ordinary dependence.
The next question asks whether people sent that water down or God did, matching the source question attached to مَاءٍ مَعِينٍ in the section.
A drink of boiling water and painful punishment are placed in one sentence, bringing the source section’s hot drink and عَذَاب together without the sweet-water sense.
The disbelievers receive a drink of boiling water and painful punishment, another exact joining of infernal drink with the section’s punishment root.
When the people of the Fire seek relief, they are relieved with water like molten metal that scorches faces; expected refreshment becomes the evil drink itself.
The one facing Hell is given putrid water to drink, preserving the passive giving-to-drink while replacing the garden spring with a punitive source.
After eating from Zaqqum they receive a mixture of boiling water on top of it, making infernal food and hot drink one meal as in the source section.
The erring deniers eat from the tree of Zaqqum; 56:54 then supplies their boiling drink, so this ayah contributes the meal’s food.
They drink boiling water on top of Zaqqum, directly completing the same food-and-hot-drink table that the section sees in 88:5–6.
لَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ repeats the source section’s “no food except” construction while changing the sole infernal food from dariʿ to foul discharge.
Choking food and painful punishment are named together, a compact parallel to the source section’s inedible infernal fare and greater punishment.
The command pours “the punishment of boiling water” over the sinner’s head, fusing عَذَاب and scalding water in one expression.
The only drink allowed in Hell is boiling water and foul fluid; its restrictive exception reverses the freely available garden cup at 78:34.

Guests must not wait for the meal’s إِنَاهُ, its readiness, and must disperse once they have eaten, طَعِمْتُمْ; one table carries both the endpoint sense behind hot ءَانِيَة and the section’s food root.
God “raised” the heaven and “set down” the balance in one ayah, directly staging the lexical opposition رَفَعَ and وَضَعَ that the section hears between raised couches and placed cups.
Purifying rain is used to revive land and give many animals and humans drink, identifying fresh drinking water as purposeful provision.
God says “We gave you sweet water to drink,” making the provided drink fresh and palatable rather than the endpoint-hot drink of punishment.
Livestock supply both what people are given to drink and what they eat, concretely joining drinking and feeding within one provided source.
Pure milk is brought from a hidden place between waste and blood and is palatable to drinkers, sharpening the section’s questions of source, purity, and ease of drinking.
Their Lord Himself gives them a purifying drink, making the ultimate giver explicit and reversing the punitive giving-to-drink in 88:5.
The sealed nectar is mixed from Tasnim, and 83:28 then identifies Tasnim as a spring; this ayah supplies the drink’s spring-derived mixture.
The righteous drink a camphor-mixed cup, whose underlying spring is disclosed in 76:6; cup and source form one continuous garden image.
The source section’s dictionary sense عَذْب appears as one sea’s fresh sweetness, explicitly bounded from the salty, bitter sea despite their meeting.
One sea is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and easy to drink while the other is salty and bitter; the ayah states the water-quality boundary behind the section’s sweet-versus-punitive wordplay.
God could make the water people drink bitterly salty, so a welcome cup depends on the same giver who can alter its quality.
A thirsty person takes a mirage for water but finds none on arrival; it directly illuminates the section’s closing reversal in which anticipated good water fails the expectant face.
The garden inhabitants call for abundant fruit and drink, whereas the source section emphasizes cups already placed within reach before a request; the two scenes mark different modes of readiness.
Pharaoh’s people are expelled from gardens and springs, showing the same attractive scene as a worldly possession that can be removed rather than a settled reward.
The drowned people leave behind gardens and springs; the shared scene becomes evidence of forfeited provision rather than enduring garden hospitality.
The earth is burst into springs until its water meets the descending flood at a decreed event; gushing water here overwhelms, bounding the controlled and welcoming garden spring.
Garden and silk are the recompense for patience, supplying the reward frame in which the silver vessels and cups of 76:15 are served.
The glass vessels are silver and precisely measured, adding fitted measure to the cups circulated in 76:15.
Immortal youths circulate around the garden people, identifying the service that bears the cups and ewers named in the next ayah.
The drink from the preceding flowing source causes neither headache nor loss of reason, a bodily reversal of the harmful waters on the section’s punitive side.
Chosen fruit follows the cup from the flowing source, contributing food to the garden table whose drink appears at 56:18.
Desired bird meat completes the food side of the service begun with cups and a cup from مَعِين.
The cup from the preceding flowing source is white and delightful to drinkers, specifying the attractive quality withheld from the hot spring.
The garden drink has no corrupting harm and does not exhaust or intoxicate, marking a concrete boundary from harmful infernal drink.
The sealed drink’s seal is musk and becomes an object of competition; this develops the “sealed” property named in 83:25 rather than leaving it an empty epithet.
Everlasting youths circulate among the garden people, supplying the attendants implicit in the circulation of vessels at 76:15.
Youths kept for the garden people circulate among them, extending the shared cup scene of 52:23 into ready service.
The garden command joins eating and pleasant drinking as recompense for deeds, a positive table opposite the hot drink and dariʿ table.
The people of the right are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they sent ahead, reversing the restrictive and painful meal in the source section.
The righteous are told to eat and drink pleasantly because of their deeds, making the garden table a reward rather than a punishment.
Abundant garden fruit is eaten after the golden dishes and cups of 43:71, so the circulating vessels belong to a full table.
This ayah identifies the denied place as the Hell rejected by the criminals; 55:44 then describes their movement between it and endpoint-hot water.
The God-fearing are amid gardens and springs in safety, a concise recurrence of the garden-spring scene.
The God-fearing dwell in gardens and springs, setting the same objects inside the secure reward announced in the preceding ayah.
The God-fearing are in gardens and springs, another direct recurrence of the reward scene defined by place and water source.
The God-fearing are among shades and springs, pairing shelter with the available water source on the garden side.
Mary and her son are sheltered on high ground with stable lodging and مَعِين, using the section’s visible flowing-water word for a worldly refuge.
Dhu al-Qarnayn reaches the sun’s setting place and finds it setting at a murky spring; it preserves عَيْن as a spring while moving it outside drinking and afterlife reward.
Water bursts as rivers from some stones and emerges when others split, giving a concrete divine precedent for water released from an apparently closed source.
Rain makes valleys flow according to their measure, so moving water appears as apportioned flow rather than a static supply.
A river is made to flow between two productive gardens, a worldly version of garden abundance organized around moving water.
Hud reminds his people that their Lord aided them with gardens and springs, presenting the shared scene as a provision that calls for recognition.
Salih’s warning names gardens and springs among the abundance in which his people expect security, placing the scene at the boundary between gift and accountability.
Abundant water would be given to drink if the people remained straight on the way, making plentiful water a conditional divine provision.
God sends purifying water from the sky; the next ayah states that it revives land and is given to creatures to drink.
Water sent from the sky supplies human drink and vegetation for grazing, joining drinking water to the wider food provision generated by one source.
Water is driven to barren land and brings forth crops eaten by livestock and people, tracing hidden water movement into food.
A rhetorical question names God as the sender of water that grows delightful gardens people could not grow themselves, matching the section’s question about who supplies flowing water.
Mary is consoled with a stream placed beneath her, a ready water source whose food-and-drink use is stated at 19:26.
Mary is told to eat and drink beside the divinely supplied stream, another concrete joining of nourishment and water in one prepared setting.
Different adjoining gardens and fruits are watered with one water yet differ in taste and quality, an inverse structural parallel to two springs sharing a name while their qualities diverge.
The people of Hell eat from Zaqqum and fill their bellies; the next ayah adds the boiling mixture that turns it into the section’s infernal meal.
The deniers fill their bellies with Zaqqum before drinking boiling water, emphasizing the food portion of the paired punishment.
They drink the boiling water like desperately thirsty camels, developing the manner of drinking after 56:54 identifies the liquid.
The passage calls this food and drink their hospitality on the Day of Judgment, confirming that the preceding punishments form an offered table.
The tree of Zaqqum supplies the object whose next ayah calls it the sinner’s food, beginning another infernal meal scene.
Zaqqum is “the food of the sinner,” a direct counterpart to the exclusive dariʿ food before its boiling quality is described.
The sinner’s food boils like boiling water, letting the hot-water image enter the food itself before 44:48 pours boiling punishment over him.
Only sinners eat the foul food named at 69:36, specifying the eaters of that restrictive infernal fare.
The condemned person gulps the putrid water but can scarcely swallow it; this makes ease of drinking a sharp boundary from sweet, palatable water.
Boiling water is poured over the heads of the people of the Fire; the same hot liquid becomes external punishment rather than a drink.
The poured boiling water melts what is inside their bellies and their skins, specifying the bodily effect of the hot source in 22:19.
The people of Hell are commanded to taste boiling water and foul cold fluid, another paired punitive beverage scene.
The condemned are dragged through boiling water and then burned, showing the hot water as an environment of punishment rather than a cup.
Hell offers neither coolness nor drink; the exception in 78:25 then reveals boiling water as the only “drink,” reversing normal refreshment.
God set the earth down for creatures, using the source section’s وَضَعَ root for deliberate availability on a larger scale than cups placed within reach.
Raised furnishings reappear within a garden inventory, preserving the “raised” side of the placement opposition that structures the cups beside raised couches in surah 88.
أَلَمْ يَأْنِ asks whether the due moment has arrived, preserving the reached-time or endpoint sense behind the source section’s description of ءَانِيَة as heat brought to its limit.

The people of the Fire ask the people of the Garden to pour down water or other provision, and are told that both are forbidden to them; the two communities and their radically different access to water meet in one exchange.

The opponents demand that the Prophet make a spring gush from the earth, closely paralleling the garden servants’ ability to make their spring gush while changing that gift into a challenge for proof.
The demand continues with a garden of palms and grapes through which rivers must be made to gush abundantly, combining garden, flowing water, and human command of its course.

God makes a spring or fountain of molten copper flow for Solomon; the same spring-and-flow form carries a non-water substance, marking a concrete boundary around the section’s drinking springs and recalling molten punitive drink.
The ayah directly asks whether the garden’s hospitality or the tree of Zaqqum is better, setting the two tables against each other before the infernal food and boiling mixture are described.

Joseph places the drinking vessel, السِّقَايَة, in his brother’s baggage; the drinking object and deliberate placement converge as in the source image, but here the placement initiates a test rather than garden service.

Giving drink to pilgrims is treated as an organized human service and then weighed against faith and striving, extending the source section’s س ق ي act from divine afterlife provision to worldly hospitality.
Fruit and desired meat are supplied immediately before the companions pass a cup at 52:23, contributing the food half of that garden table.
Desired fruits stand between the garden springs of 77:41 and the command to eat and drink at 77:43, explicitly connecting source, food, and consumption.
The high garden’s fruit clusters are brought near before its people are told to eat and drink, a close parallel to cups placed within reach before they are requested.

Garden shade is brought near and fruit clusters are lowered within easy reach immediately before the vessels and cups are circulated, extending the section’s image of provision already positioned for use.
Gardens and grapes contribute the food setting whose brimming cup appears at 78:34, helping form the positive table opposed to the boiling drink earlier in the surah.
Each of the two gardens contains two kinds of every fruit after their two flowing springs are named, extending the paired-water image into paired provision.
Fruit, palms, and pomegranates follow the two gushing springs, supplying the food side of the second garden-and-spring scene.
The garden inhabitants receive fruit and honor before the cup from a flowing source is passed to them at 37:45, so the drink belongs to a supplied table.
The sinner’s food is likened to molten substance boiling in bellies, supplying the internal heat between its identification as food and its comparison with boiling water.
A rhetorical question asks who sends water from the sky and revives the earth, and the addressees answer “God”; it repeats the section’s demand to acknowledge the giver behind available water.
God sends water from the sky in due measure and revives dead land with it, adding measured provision and renewal to the section’s moving-water side.
